title: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
paragraphs: On this exchange study abroad I did clerkships for two months at The Chinese University of Hong Kong. The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, under the "one country, two systems" principle, retains systems from British rule and has English among its official languages, so it is an easy city to live in even for foreigners who cannot speak Chinese. Prices were somewhat high, but public safety was the same as or better than in Japan, and I could walk around alone until late at night without worry.

In Hong Kong there were a great many people who like Japan. Among the doctors and local students I talked with, there was no one who had not been to Japan, and during the clerkship I was often greeted in Japanese with things like "ohayou gozaimasu." Studying Cantonese so as not to be outdone by their Japanese is also a good memory. The population of Hong Kong is about 7.5 million, and I heard that in 2017 and 2018 more than 2 million Hong Kong people visited Japan in a year, so I strongly felt how high the interest in Japan is. Even outside the hospital I was often welcomed just for being Japanese, and once a complete stranger treated me to char siu. Since I was living alone as a foreigner, this was truly reassuring.

I did my clerkship in gastroenterology at Prince of Wales Hospital, the teaching hospital of The Chinese University of Hong Kong. I mainly observed endoscopy, outpatient clinics and rounds, and I was also allowed to attend an academic conference several times. The charts were written in English, and rounds and conferences were also in English, so I had no trouble with language.

In observing endoscopy, I was able to see a full range of procedures, including some I could not see in Japan. A characteristic was that not only physicians but also surgeons of all kinds performed many endoscopic examinations, ERCP, EUS and endoscopic resections. I was told that even now it is probably rare in other countries for surgeons to do this much endoscopy. Among the many types of endoscopic procedures, the one that differed most between Hong Kong and Japan was, unexpectedly, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. In Japan, I think they often take dozens of photographs and use NBI regardless of whether there is a lesion, but in Hong Kong they did not take photographs of parts without lesions and rarely used NBI. I was shocked that when there was no particular abnormality, the examination really ended very quickly.

In observing outpatient clinics, the doctors immediately translated the important points, and when local students were with me they interpreted simultaneously, so I could do the clerkship without problems. Partly because the number of patients was large, I could study many rare diseases such as IgG4-related disease, as well as severe cases of IBD. In free time in the outpatient clinic, they also gave lectures for local students and we discussed differences in the drugs and treatments used in Hong Kong and Japan. I had known before going to Hong Kong that the patients speak Cantonese, so to be honest I did not expect much from observing outpatient clinics, but when I went I found I could talk calmly with the doctors, and it was my favorite time in the clerkship.

The doctors of gastroenterology were very friendly to me and took me many times to lunches and dinners at hot pot and local restaurants. Moreover, after I returned to Japan, an Assistant Professor from gastroenterology came to Nagoya with a friend, and we went sightseeing and ate teppanyaki together.

It was also impressive that many foreign gastroenterologists from Europe and Asia came for endoscopy training and study. I was told that it is not so difficult for foreign doctors to practise endoscopy at Prince of Wales Hospital, and they often asked me whether they could train in endoscopy in the same way in Japan. Since I often observed endoscopy and ate lunch at the hospital with them, I could talk with doctors from various countries, which was very meaningful.

Talking with doctors from Hong Kong and other countries, I felt that Japanese endoscopy and surgery attract attention from around the world. I was asked, even though I was still a student, "You do it like this in Japan too, right?", and told that Japan is the most advanced in the gastroenterology field. I was also impressed that a surgeon said he is amazed when he sees Japanese surgeons operate at academic conferences. I was often told the names of famous Japanese doctors, including professors of Nagoya University, and I felt proud to be Japanese.

The healthcare system in Hong Kong is very different from Japan's. Residents of Hong Kong can visit and be admitted to public hospitals more cheaply than in Japan, but for that reason the wards were crowded, appointments could not be had for months, and waiting times in outpatient clinics were also quite long. I cannot forget the sight of beds lined up even in the corridors outside the rooms, all full. Even so, I never saw an inpatient or outpatient complaining to a doctor.

I also often talked with local students and went sightseeing, for example to an outlying island by ferry, with international students from other countries. The international students were all from Europe and I was the only Japanese. I had the chance to talk with people from various countries and could feel differences from Japanese people in thinking and tastes, and I feel that my horizons broadened.

Until this exchange study abroad, I had never lived alone, traveled abroad alone or studied abroad, and before leaving I was very anxious about whether I could live on my own. But the doctors in Hong Kong, local students, other international students, and local people outside the hospital were all kind to me and I could live comfortably. Because it was a clinical clerkship abroad, it may be off its purpose, but the biggest change in me from studying abroad is that when I meet people from abroad in Japan from now on, I have come to want to talk to them and look after them as much as I can.

Finally, I am truly grateful to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the professors of the International Collaboration Office, who supported me from the preparation for studying abroad through to after it, and to the professors of The Chinese University of Hong Kong. Thank you very much.
